Problem:

title: Good PRD: specific user, sorted requirements, maths that adds up, the twist handled
context:
Problem card (Food and drink): Snacks go stale fast in humid coastal towns. Small shops in towns like Udupi and Alappuzha throw away up to a fifth of their packaged snacks because opened and even sealed packs go soft within days in the monsoon.

The twist: From 1 January, single-use plastic packaging under 50 microns is banned across the state.
text:
Crisp Coast (CRSP)

Problem:
In Udupi and Mangaluru, a typical kirana shop stocks about 300 snack packs and, by its owners' own count in our talks with 12 shops, loses 40 to 60 of them a month in the monsoon to softness. At an average of Rs 20 a pack that is Rs 800 to Rs 1,200 a month, close to a tenth of a small shop's snack margin.

Target user:
Owners of small kirana shops (one counter, no air conditioning) in coastal towns of Karnataka and Kerala, who restock snacks weekly from a distributor.

Must have:
A refillable counter jar with a gasket lid that keeps a week of loose snacks crisp. A paper-and-cellulose bag for each sale (no plastic, in line with the January ban). Weekly refills of loose snacks delivered with the shop's usual restock.

Should have:
A small sticker that changes colour when the jar's humidity is too high. Two jar sizes.

Not in version 1:
Our own snack brand; home delivery; an app.

Per-pack maths:
Refill of 2 kg sold to the shop at Rs 640 (Rs 32 per 100 g). Our cost: snacks Rs 420, cellulose bags Rs 60, delivery share Rs 40, total Rs 520, margin Rs 120 per refill. The shop sells 100 g at Rs 45, so it earns Rs 260 per refill instead of throwing packs away. The jar (Rs 350 to make) is lent free against a Rs 500 deposit.

Go to market:
Start with 30 shops along two distributor routes in Udupi, through the distributor, who gets Rs 20 per refill. Sign shops in the first two weeks of the monsoon, when the loss is visible.

Success metrics:
30 shops by week 4; 25 of them reorder by week 8; average shop loss falls from 50 to under 10 packs a month (counted with the owners).

Risks:
Shops may distrust loose snacks: we keep the brand names on the jar label. Cellulose bags may tear in the rain: we test three suppliers before launch. The distributor may copy us: we sign a one-season exclusive route deal.

title: Excellent PRD: evidence, sharp scope, full unit economics, tested assumptions
context:
Problem card (Food and drink): Snacks go stale fast in humid coastal towns. Small shops in towns like Udupi and Alappuzha throw away up to a fifth of their packaged snacks because opened and even sealed packs go soft within days in the monsoon.

The twist: From 1 January, single-use plastic packaging under 50 microns is banned across the state.
text:
Monsoon Fresh (MNSF)

Problem:
We visited 18 kirana shops in Udupi and Alappuzha and counted stale returns for one week in July: the median shop wrote off 14 packs a week (about 60 a month, Rs 1,150 at retail), and 15 of 18 owners said soft snacks also lose them repeat customers. The state's plastic ban from 1 January removes the cheap multilayer packs that hide the problem today, so the loss will grow.

Target user:
Owners of one-counter kirana shops without air conditioning in coastal towns of Karnataka and Kerala, selling 250 to 400 snack packs a month. Not supermarkets (they already have climate control).

Must have:
1. Sealed steel counter dispensers (3 compartments) that keep loose snacks crisp for 10 days in 85% humidity, tested by us over 3 weeks. 2. Ban-compliant cellulose bags printed with the snack and date. 3. Weekly refills on the shop's existing distributor route.

Should have:
Humidity dot on each compartment; a monthly loss report for the owner.

Not in version 1:
Our own snacks, consumer delivery, payments app, any electronics.

Per-pack maths:
Per 2 kg refill: price to shop Rs 640; cost Rs 520 (snacks 420, bags 60, distributor fee 40); our margin Rs 120. Shop margin Rs 260 per refill plus about Rs 1,000 a month of avoided write-offs. Dispenser costs Rs 900, recovered from our margin after 8 refills (about 2 months at 1 refill a week); the shop pays a Rs 500 refundable deposit. Fixed costs Rs 60,000 a month (2 people, a van share), covered at 500 refills a month, about 120 shops.

Go to market:
Phase 1 (weeks 1 to 4): 40 shops on two routes of one distributor in Udupi who agreed in writing to carry refills for Rs 40 each. Phase 2 (weeks 5 to 12): add Alappuzha routes once 30 of the first 40 shops reorder. Cost to sign a shop: about Rs 300 of our time and a free first refill.

Success metrics:
40 shops signed by week 4; at least 75% reorder by week 8; median write-offs below 3 packs a week by week 8; 120 shops (break-even) by week 16.

Risks:
Biggest assumption: owners accept loose snacks in branded dispensers; we test it first with 5 shops for 2 weeks. Cellulose bags may soften in rain: two suppliers tested, the better one chosen. Distributor dependence: a one-season exclusive deal, and our own van share as a fallback.

title: Good solution: specific diagnosis, real options, numbers that add up
context:
The rescued company's PRD (summary): Crisp Coast (CRSP) lends counter jars to coastal kirana shops and sells weekly 2 kg refills of loose snacks in cellulose bags at Rs 640 (cost Rs 520, margin Rs 120), through a distributor.

Crisis card (Supply): Your main supplier shuts down. Your only snack supplier closes overnight after a factory fire. The nearest alternative is 300 km away and charges 30% more.
text:
Diagnosis:
CRSP's whole product is the weekly refill; without snacks, jars sit empty and shops return to plastic packs within two weeks. Snacks are Rs 420 of the Rs 520 cost per refill, so a 30% rise adds Rs 126 and wipes out the Rs 120 margin. The jars, bags and distributor route are unaffected.

Three options:
A: buy from the far supplier at +30% and absorb it (keeps shops, loses about Rs 6 per refill). B: buy from the far supplier and raise the refill price by Rs 80 (keeps margin, risks shops). C: sign two small local fryers in Udupi at +12%, needing a quality check (cheaper but slower to start).

Recommendation:
C, bridged by A for three weeks: local fryers cost less in the long run and remove the single-supplier risk that caused this crisis.

Per-pack maths:
Weeks 1 to 3 (A): cost Rs 646, price Rs 640, loss Rs 6 per refill, about Rs 1,800 over 300 refills. From week 4 (C): snacks Rs 470, total cost Rs 570, price raised to Rs 660, margin Rs 90.

Timeline:
Week 1: order from the far supplier; visit four local fryers. Week 2: taste and humidity test of samples. Week 3: contracts with two fryers. Week 4: first local refills; milestone: 90% of shops keep their jars.

Risks:
Local quality may vary: weekly batch tests and two fryers instead of one. Shops may refuse Rs 20 more: we show them the write-offs they avoid.

title: Excellent solution: full diagnosis, costed options, recovery path, milestones
context:
The rescued company's PRD (summary): Crisp Coast (CRSP) lends counter jars to coastal kirana shops and sells weekly 2 kg refills of loose snacks in cellulose bags at Rs 640 (cost Rs 520, margin Rs 120), through a distributor.

Crisis card (Supply): Your main supplier shuts down. Your only snack supplier closes overnight after a factory fire. The nearest alternative is 300 km away and charges 30% more.
text:
Diagnosis:
The fire hits CRSP's only input: snacks are 81% of the refill cost (Rs 420 of Rs 520), and the jar model only works if refills arrive every week, since an empty jar sends the owner back to plastic packs and the deposit back to us. At +30% the snack cost is Rs 546, total Rs 646, a loss of Rs 6 per refill. What stays intact: the 40 shop relationships, the jars, the ban-compliant bags and the distributor route.

Three options:
A, far supplier at +30%, price unchanged: zero delay, about Rs 1,800 lost a month at 300 refills; keeps every shop. B, far supplier, refill price up Rs 80: margin restored, but shops then earn Rs 180 instead of Rs 260 per refill, and 4 of the 12 owners we called said they would stop. C, two local Udupi fryers at +12% (Rs 470), with a 2-week quality trial: margin Rs 90 at a Rs 20 price rise, and no single point of failure.

Recommendation:
C, with A as a three-week bridge, because it is the only option that both keeps the shops and fixes the cause of the crisis (one supplier). B is rejected: losing a third of the shops costs more than the bridge.

Per-pack maths:
Bridge (weeks 1 to 3): Rs 646 cost vs Rs 640 price, total loss about Rs 1,800. Local supply (week 4 on): cost Rs 470 + 60 + 40 = Rs 570; price Rs 660 (+Rs 20); margin Rs 90 per refill, Rs 27,000 a month at 300 refills. Shops still earn Rs 240 per refill. The bridge loss is recovered in under 3 days of local-supply margin.

Timeline:
Day 1: order three weeks from the far supplier; call all 40 shops. Days 2 to 7: samples from four local fryers. Week 2: humidity test (10 days in jars at 85%) and taste test with 5 owners. Week 3: contracts with the best two, 60/40 split. Week 4: first local refills. Milestone at week 6: at least 36 of 40 shops reorder and stale returns stay under 3 packs a week.

Risks:
Local batches may differ: weekly batch tests, and either fryer can cover 100% for two weeks. A fryer may raise prices after the trial: a fixed price for the season in the contract. Shops may resist Rs 20: we show each owner the write-off savings from his own loss report, and keep the old price for shops that sign for the season.
